question:
A 63-year-old male nurse visits his primary care physician following a positive interferon-gamma
release assay, which was performed as part of a routine onboarding screening. He reports prior
exposure to an individual with active tuberculosis several months ago but denies ever experiencing
symptoms. The patient is otherwise healthy and is not on any medications. Sputum analysis and chest
radiography are performed and show no abnormalities. What is the most appropriate treatment
regimen for this patient’s condition? Answer Choices: (A) Rifabutin monotherapy (B) Levofloxacin
monotherapy (C) Rifampin and pyrazinamide (D) Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide (E)
Isoniazid with pyridoxine supplementation (F) Azithromycin monotherapy (G) No treatment required
due to normal chest radiography and sputum analysis (H) Rifampin and isoniazid combination therapy
(I) Isoniazid monotherapy (J) Rifampin monotherapy
 A. Azithromycin monotherapy
B. Levofloxacin monotherapy
C. Rifampin monotherapy
D. Rifampin and pyrazinamide
E. Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide
F. Isoniazid with pyridoxine supplementation
G. Isoniazid monotherapy
H. No treatment required due to normal chest radiography and sputum analysis
I. Rifampin and isoniazid combination therapy
J. Rifabutin monotherapy
